{{Short description|Concept in geometry}}
In [[differential geometry]], a '''quaternionic manifold''' is a [[quaternion]]ic analog of a [[complex manifold]]. The definition is more complicated and technical than the one for complex manifolds due in part to the [[noncommutative|noncommutativity]] of the quaternions and in part to the lack of a suitable calculus of [[holomorphic function]]s for quaternions. The most succinct definition uses the language of [[G-structure on a manifold|''G''-structures on a manifold]]. Specifically, a '''quaternionic ''n-''manifold''' can be defined as a [[smooth manifold]] of real dimension 4''n'' equipped with a torsion-free <math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})\cdot\mathbb{H}^\times</math>-structure. More naïve, but straightforward, definitions lead to a dearth of examples, and exclude spaces like [[quaternionic projective space]] which should clearly be considered as quaternionic manifolds.

== Early history ==

[[Marcel Berger]]'s 1955 paper<ref>{{cite journal |first=Marcel |last=Berger |title=Sur les groups d'holonomie des variétés à connexion affine et des variétés riemanniennes |journal=Bull. Soc. Math. France |volume=83 |issue= |pages=279–330 |year=1955 |doi=10.24033/bsmf.1464 |url=http://www.numdam.org/article/BSMF_1955__83__279_0.pdf |doi-access=free }}</ref> on the classification of Riemannian holonomy groups first raised the issue of the existence of non-symmetric manifolds with holonomy Sp(''n'')·Sp(1).Interesting results were proved in the mid-1960s in pioneering work by [[Edmond Bonan]]<ref>{{cite journal |first=Edmond |last=Bonan |title=Structure presque quaternale sur une variété differentiable |journal=Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences |volume=261 |issue= |pages=5445–8 |year=1965 }}</ref> and Kraines<ref>{{cite journal |first=Vivian Yoh |last=Kraines |title=Topology of quaternionic manifolds |journal= Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=122 |issue=2 |pages=357–367 |year=1966 
|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1966-0192513-X |jstor=1994553 |url=https://www.ams.org/tran/1966-122-02/S0002-9947-1966-0192513-X/S0002-9947-1966-0192513-X.pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref> who have independently proven that any such manifold admits a parallel 4-form <math>\Omega</math>.The long-awaited analog of strong Lefschetz theorem was published <ref>{{cite journal|first=Edmond | last=Bonan|title=Sur l'algèbre extérieure d'une variété presque hermitienne quaternionique |journal= Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences|volume =295|year=1982|pages=115–118}}</ref> in 1982 :     <math>                                                            
 \Omega^{n-k}\wedge\bigwedge^{2k}T^*M=\bigwedge^{4n-2k}T^*M.</math>

==Definitions==

===The enhanced quaternionic general linear group===

If we regard the [[quaternionic vector space]] <math>\mathbb{H}^n\cong\R^{4n}</math> as a [[right module|right <math>\mathbb{H}</math>-module]], we can identify the algebra of right <math>\mathbb{H}</math>-linear maps with the algebra of <math>n\times n</math> [[quaternionic matrix|quaternionic matrices]] acting on <math>\mathbb{H}^n</math> ''from the left''. The invertible right <math>\mathbb{H}</math>-linear maps then form a subgroup <math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})</math> of <math>\operatorname{GL}(4n, \R)</math>. We can enhance this group with the group <math>\mathbb{H}^\times</math> of nonzero quaternions acting by scalar multiplication on <math>\mathbb{H}^n</math> ''from the right''. Since this scalar multiplication is <math>\R</math>-linear (but ''not'' <math>\mathbb{H}</math>-linear) we have another embedding of <math>\mathbb{H}^\times</math> into <math>\operatorname{GL}(4n, \R)</math>. The group <math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})\cdot\mathbb{H}^\times</math> is then defined as the product of these subgroups in <math>\operatorname{GL}(4n, \R)</math>. Since the intersection of the subgroups <math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})</math> and <math>\mathbb{H}^\times</math> in <math>\operatorname{GL}(4n, \R)</math> is their mutual center <math>\R^\times</math> (the group of scalar matrices with nonzero real coefficients), we have the isomorphism
:<math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})\cdot\mathbb{H}^\times \cong (\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})\times\mathbb{H}^\times)/\R^\times.</math>

===Almost quaternionic structure===

An '''almost quaternionic structure''' on a smooth manifold <math>M</math> is just a <math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})\cdot\mathbb{H}^\times</math>-structure on <math>M</math>. Equivalently, it can be defined as a [[subbundle]] <math>H</math> of the [[endomorphism bundle]] <math>\operatorname{End}(TM)</math> such that each fiber <math>H_x</math> is isomorphic (as a [[algebra over a field|real algebra]]) to the [[quaternions|quaternion algebra]] <math>\mathbb{H}</math>. The subbundle <math>H</math> is called the '''almost quaternionic structure bundle'''. A manifold equipped with an almost quaternionic structure is called an '''almost quaternionic manifold'''.

The quaternion structure bundle <math>H</math> naturally admits a [[bundle metric]] coming from the quaternionic algebra structure, and, with this metric, <math>H</math> splits into an orthogonal [[Whitney sum|direct sum]] of vector bundles
<math>H = L\oplus E</math>
where <math>L</math> is the trivial line bundle through the identity operator, and <math>E</math> is a rank-3 vector bundle corresponding to the purely imaginary quaternions. Neither the bundles <math>H</math> or <math>E</math> are necessarily trivial.

The [[sphere bundle|unit sphere bundle]]
<math>Z = S(E)</math>
inside <math>E</math> corresponds to the pure unit imaginary quaternions. These are endomorphisms of the tangent spaces that square to −1. The bundle <math>Z</math> is called the '''twistor space''' of the manifold <math>M</math>, and its properties are described in more detail below. [[section (fiber bundle)|Local section]]s of <math>Z</math> are (locally defined) [[almost complex structure]]s. There exists a neighborhood <math>U</math> of every point <math>x</math> in an almost quaternionic manifold <math>M</math> with an entire [[2-sphere]] of almost complex structures defined on <math>U</math>. One can always find <math>I, J, K\in\Gamma(Z|_U)</math> such that 
:<math>I^2 = J^2 = K^2 = IJK = -1</math>
Note, however, that none of these operators may be extendable to all of <math>M</math>. That is, the bundle <math>Z</math> may admit no ''global'' sections (e.g. this is the case with [[quaternionic projective space]] <math>\mathbb{HP}^n</math>). This is in marked contrast to the situation for complex manifolds, which always have a globally defined almost complex structure.

===Quaternionic structure===

A '''quaternionic structure''' on a smooth manifold <math>M</math> is an almost quaternionic structure <math>Q</math> which admits a [[torsion tensor|torsion-free]] [[affine connection]] <math>\nabla</math> preserving <math>Q</math>. Such a connection is never unique, and is not considered to be part of the quaternionic structure.  A '''quaternionic manifold''' is a smooth manifold <math>M</math> together with a quaternionic structure on <math>M</math>.

==Special cases and additional structures==

===Hypercomplex manifolds===

A '''[[hypercomplex manifold]]''' is a quaternionic manifold with a torsion-free <math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})</math>-structure. The reduction of the structure group to <math>\operatorname{GL}(n, \mathbb{H})</math> is possible if and only if the almost quaternionic structure bundle <math>H\subset \operatorname{End}(TM)</math> is trivial (i.e. isomorphic to <math>M\times\mathbb{H}</math>). An almost hypercomplex structure corresponds to a global frame of <math>H</math>, or, equivalently, triple of almost complex structures <math>I, J</math>, and <math>K</math> such that
:<math>I^2 = J^2 = K^2 = IJK = -1</math>
A hypercomplex structure is an almost hypercomplex structure such that each of <math>I, J</math>, and <math>K</math> are integrable. 

===Quaternionic Kähler manifolds===

A '''[[quaternionic Kähler manifold]]''' is a quaternionic manifold with a torsion-free <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)\cdot\operatorname{Sp}(1)</math>-structure.

===Hyperkähler manifolds===

A '''[[hyperkähler manifold]]''' is a quaternionic manifold with a torsion-free <math>\operatorname{Sp}(n)</math>-structure. A hyperkähler manifold is simultaneously a hypercomplex manifold and a quaternionic Kähler manifold.

==Twistor space==

Given a quaternionic <math>n</math>-manifold <math>M</math>, the unit 2-sphere subbundle <math>Z=S(E)</math> corresponding to the pure unit imaginary quaternions (or almost complex structures) is called the '''twistor space''' of <math>M</math>. It turns out that, when <math>n\ge 2</math>, there exists a natural [[complex manifold|complex structure]] on <math>Z</math> such that the fibers of the projection <math>Z\to M</math> are isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{CP}^1</math>. When <math>n=1</math>, the space <math>Z</math> admits a natural [[almost complex structure]], but this structure is integrable only if the manifold is [[self-dual manifold|self-dual]]. It turns out that the quaternionic geometry on <math>M</math> can be reconstructed entirely from holomorphic data on <math>Z</math>.

The twistor space theory gives a method of translating problems on quaternionic manifolds into problems on complex manifolds, which are much better understood, and amenable to methods from [[algebraic geometry]]. Unfortunately, the twistor space of a quaternionic manifold can be quite complicated, even for simple spaces like <math>\mathbb{H}^n</math>.
